Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
- 24-year-old woman with 2-day midline lower abdominal pain, mild urinary frequency, and slight hematuria; suspected urinary tract infection (UTI); empirical 3-day oral antibiotics prescribed.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Lower abdominal pain for 2 days, midline.
- Associated symptoms: Feels hot/sweaty; measured temp ~37 °C; mild nausea (no vomiting); slight pink discoloration in urine; mild ↑ urinary frequency; increased thirst; no dysuria, flank/back pain, vaginal discharge, or acid reflux.
- Bowel habit: Constipated last week, now normal; last bowel movement 2 h prior, normal, no blood.
- Past medical history: No significant chronic conditions. Previous contraceptive implant removed ~1 yr ago.
- Allergies: Amoxicillin (type of reaction not documented).
- Medications: None regular; no OTC.
- Family history: Mother had early-stage breast cancer (treated).
- Social / preventive: Lives with parents; non-smoker; drinks ~1 beer on 4 days/week; no recent travel; regular menses, no inter-menstrual or post-coital bleeding.

Examination:
- Vitals: Patient-reported temperature 37 °C (self-check).
- No physical examination documented.

Impression:
- Likely uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection.

Plan:
- Prescribe oral antibiotic course: “twice daily for 3 days” (drug and dose not specified).
  • Note: patient allergic to amoxicillin—ensure non-penicillin agent selected.
- Start antibiotic as soon as dispensed at allocated pharmacy.
- Safety-net advice: Return/seek care if worsening pain, fever, back pain, new symptoms, or recurrence; may require face-to-face assessment.
- No additional tests or referrals planned at this time.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements:
  – Drug name, dose, route for antibiotic.
  – Type of allergic reaction to amoxicillin.
  – Medication reconciliation confirmation.
  – Objective vitals, abdominal and pelvic exam, urinalysis, pregnancy test.
● Internal conflicts: None noted.
● Transcript quality: Clear; occasional minor inaudible words but key clinical data understandable.
